81--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
82---     `INCOMING BOCHUM MATERIAL summarized by Claude (old/bochum-lf-updates/AltAuto.v): the
83---        Bochum LF updates extend AltAuto's discussion of the sequencing
84---        tactical with new material on Rocq's "local form with `..`":
85---
86---          T; [T1 .. | Tn]
87---
88---        which applies T1 to the first goal, Tn to the last, and T1 to all
89---        goals in between (variants: T; [T1 | .. | Tn] applies nothing in
90---        between; the `..` may also appear first, last, or alone).  The new
91---        material illustrates this by revisiting star_app from IndProp:
92---
93---          Lemma star_app'': forall T (s1 s2 : list T) (re : reg_exp T),
94---            s1 =~ Star re ->
95---            s2 =~ Star re ->
96---            s1 ++ s2 =~ Star re.
97---          Proof.
98---            intros T s1 s2 re H1.
99---            remember (Star re) as re' eqn:Eq.
100---            induction H1
101---              as [|x'|s1 re1 s2' re2 Hmatch1 IH1 Hmatch2 IH2
102---                  |s1 re1 re2 Hmatch IH|re1 s2' re2 Hmatch IH
103---                  |re''|s1 s2' re'' Hmatch1 IH1 Hmatch2 IH2];
104---              [discriminate .. | intros H; apply H | idtac]. (* <=== *)
105---            (* MStarApp *)
106---            intros H1. rewrite <- app_assoc.
107---            apply MStarApp.
108---            + apply Hmatch1.
109---            + apply IH2.
110---              * apply Eq.
111---              * apply H1.
112---          Qed.
113---
114---        (first shown in its long form with all seven cases spelled out, then
115---        shortened as above).  Bochum also adds a QUIETSOLUTION alternate
116---        solution to AltAuto's re_opt exercise that uses nested `..` lists
117---        instead of `try`, and rewords the introduction of `T; T'` to say
118---        simply that it is "equivalent to locally performing T' on all the
119---        subgoals".
120---
121---        To incorporate: Lean has no direct analogue of the positional
122---        `[T1 .. | Tn]` goal-selector list; the closest idioms are
123---        case-labelled alternatives (`case ... =>`/`next`), `all_goals`,
124---        and `first`.  A future pass should decide whether to add a
125---        parallel discussion here (e.g. using `star_app` below, proving the
126---        six non-MStarApp cases uniformly) or to record the Rocq material
127---        as intentionally unported.`

119--- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like
120--- `||` and `&&` are defined with specified precedence and
121--- associativity. For example, the `infixl` directive above
122--- states that `&&` is an infix operator, has precedence 35,
123--- and is left-associative, while `||` is also infix and
124--- left-associative and has precedence 30. This means that
125--- `MyBool.true || MyBool.false && MyBool.false` is parsed as
126--- `MyBool.true || (MyBool.false && MyBool.false)`.
127-
128--- Custom notations are defined using the `notation`, `infixl`,

130--- will see (again, in skippable sections) later on.

649+-- Trying to carry out this proof by induction on `n` when `m`
650+-- is already in the context doesn't work because we are then
651+-- trying to prove a statement involving *every* `n` but just a
652+-- *particular* `m`.
653+
654+-- A successful proof of `double_injective` keeps `m`
655+-- universally quantified in the goal statement at the point
656+-- where the `induction` tactic is invoked on `n`.
657+
658+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
659+--     The comments in this proof might need trimming --
660+--     probably not appropriate in the terse version, and
661+--     probably not nicely typeset in the full version
662+
663+theorem double_injective : ∀ (n m : Nat),
664+    n.double = m.double →
665+    n = m := by
666+  intro n
667+  induction n
668+  case zero =>
669+    rw [Nat.double_zero]
670+    intro m eq
671+    cases m
672+    case zero => rfl
673+    case succ _ =>
674+      rw [Nat.double_succ] at eq
675+      contradiction
676+  case succ n' ih =>
677+  -- Notice that both the goal and the induction hypothesis are
678+  -- different this time: the goal asks us to prove something more
679+  -- general (i.e., we must prove the statement for _every_ `m`), but
680+  -- the induction hypothesis `ih` is correspondingly more flexible,
681+  -- allowing us to choose any `m` we like when we apply it.
682+  intro m eq
683+  -- Now we've introduced the assumption that `double n = double m`.
684+  -- Since we are doing a case analysis on `n`, we also need a case
685+  -- analysis on `m` to keep the two in sync.
686+  cases m
687+  case zero =>
688+    -- The 0 case is trivial:
689+    rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
690+    contradiction
691+  case succ m' =>
692+    congr
693+    -- Since we are now in the second branch of the `cases m`, the
694+    -- `m'` mentioned in the context is the predecessor of the `m` we
695+    -- started out talking about.  Since we are also in the `succ` branch of
696+    -- the induction, this is perfect: if we instantiate the generic `m`
697+    -- in the IH with the current `m'` (this instantiation is performed
698+    -- automatically by the `apply` in the next step), then `ih` gives
699+    -- us exactly what we need to finish the proof.
700+    apply ih; rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at eq; injections
701+

703+--     `HIDE: Robert Rand: I found jumping straight to "what if we want to
704+--     do induction on the second argument" via double_injective_take2_FAILED
705+--     to be much more natural here.`
706+
707+-- The thing to take away from all this is that you need to be
708+-- careful, when using induction, that you are not trying to
709+-- prove something too specific: When proving a property
710+-- quantified over variables `n` and `m` by induction on `n`,
711+-- it is sometimes crucial to leave `m` "generic."

781+-- We'll use a boolean "less or equal" test on numbers, written
782+-- `n ≤? m` (the library function `Nat.ble`), together with the
783+-- fact that it commutes with successor on both sides.
784+
785+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
786+--     Added, to make the file compile, on Claude's suggestion.
787+--     But is this the right way? Answer: No, just replaces
788+--     uses of it by Nat.ble!
789+
790+infix:52 " ≤? " => Nat.ble
791+
792+theorem zero_ble (m : Nat) : (0 ≤? m) = true := rfl
793+theorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ((n + 1) ≤? (m + 1)) = (n ≤? m) := rfl
794+
795+-- Note to developers (Claude, before next release):
796+--     Claude-generated note. (BCP: Whoever reviews this part
797+--     of the chapter next should read and delete it.)
798+--
799+--     The `leb_*` → `ble_*` rename is now applied across
800+--     `Lists`, `Tactics`, and `Logic`, matching the
801+--     `ble_complete` / `ble_correct` / `ble_iff` names already
802+--     used in `IndProp`: every one of these is stated over
803+--     `≤?`, which is notation for `Nat.ble` (declared just
804+--     above), so the name now tracks the function. Statements
805+--     keep the `≤?` notation rather than spelling out
806+--     `Nat.ble`, following `IndProp`.
807+--
808+--     One thing to think about: `beq_succ` (above, and used in
809+--     `Logic`) is a separate `BEq` question: it could likewise
810+--     be restated via `Nat.beq_eq_true_eq` / `BEq.comm`, which
811+--     would let the `beq_symm` exercise below drop its
812+--     induction. Worth a decision, but it changes an
813+--     exercise's shape, not just a name.
814+
815+-- Suppose that we want to show that `add` is the inverse of
816+-- `sub`. Since we are working with natural numbers, we need an
817+-- assumption to prevent `sub` from truncating its result. With
818+-- this assumption, the induction hypothesis becomes
819+-- `forall m, n' ≤? m = true → (m - n') + n' = m`. The
820+-- beginning of the proof uses techniques we have already seen
821+-- -- in particular, notice how we induct on `n` before
822+-- introducing `m`, so that the induction hypothesis becomes
823+-- sufficiently general.
824+
825+theorem sub_add_ble : ∀ (n m : Nat),
826+    n ≤? m = true → (m - n) + n = m := by
827+  intro n
828+  induction n
829+  case zero =>
830+    intro m h; rw [add_zero]; cases m
831+    case zero => rfl
832+    case succ => rfl
833+  case succ n' ih =>
834+    intro m h; cases m
835+    case zero => contradiction
836+    case succ m' =>
837+      rw [succ_ble_succ] at h
838+      rw [succ_sub_succ, add_succ]
839+    -- At this point, we need to show `(m' - n') + n' + 1 = m' + 1`
840+    -- from the assumption `(n' <= m') = true`.  We could use the
841+    -- `have` tactic to prove `(m' - n') + n' = m'` from the IH.
842+    -- However, we can also just use `rw` directly...
843+      rw [ih]
844+      assumption

928+      rw [h'] at eq; dsimp at eq
929+      contradiction
930+    case true =>
931+      apply beq_eq at h'
932+      rw [h']; rfl
933+      -- When we come to the second equality test in the body
934+      -- of the function we are reasoning about, we can use
935+      -- `h:` again in the same way, allowing us to finish the
936+      -- proof.
937+  case true =>
938+    apply beq_eq at h
939+    rw [h]; rfl
940+
941+-- Micro Sermon
942+
943+-- Mindless proof-hacking is a terrible temptation...
944+
945+-- Try to resist!

407-namespace Algebra
408-
409--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in
410--- Lean to define mathematical structures that carry both
411--- operators and laws about how those operators interact. As a
412--- simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a *monoid*,
413--- a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
414-
415--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
416-
417--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
418---   combines two elements of type `α` into one,
419-
420--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the
421---   "identity element", and
422-
423--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely
424---   that:
425-
426---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
427-
428---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
429---     associative)
430-
431--- We can express these requirements in the form of a
432--- typeclass:
433-
434--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
435-class OpSet (α : Type) where
436-  op : α → α → α
437-
438-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
439-
440-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
441-  id : α
442-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
443-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
444-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
445-
446--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass
447--- extends the `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with
448--- an operator and some notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass
449--- "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`, similar to how a class
450--- would in an object-oriented language.
451-

453--- monoid, where `0` is the identity element. Note that we
454--- don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet` instance separately, we
455--- can define a single instance that implements both classes.
456-

489--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also
490--- prove some properties about monoids in general, just based
491--- on the laws defined on the typeclass. One simple theorem
492--- about monoids is that the identity element of a monoid is
493--- unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set
494--- with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
495--- the same:
496-
497-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
498-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
499-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
500-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
501-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
502-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
503-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
504-    rw [h]
505-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
506-    rw [right_id₂]
507-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
508-  exact h'
509-
510--- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances
511--- `m₁` and `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic
512--- chapter. When we do so however, because these are class
513--- instances instead of normal structures, we preface our tuple
514--- with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above proof,
515--- if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can
516--- set `set_option pp.all true` or
517--- `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you more
518--- clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed
519--- as `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂`
520--- are implicit arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting
521--- `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
522--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

335--- alternative characterization that works better with
